extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, patent examiners, and students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how a patent specification must be written to satisfy legal requirements (what to disclose, how much detail, audiences, and what renders a specification insufficient or void). Focuses on enablement, written description, best mode, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three required subjects of the description
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must contain full explanations of three different subjects: (1) the invention itself; (2) the manner of making, constructing, and operating it; and (3) the mode of putting it to practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete knowledge of all three points is necessary to render the invention available to the public without further experiment or inventive skill. The description should be confined to these three points; other narrative or advertising matter is surplusage and objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — must enable one skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must be full, clear, and exact so as to enable one skilled in the art or science to make, construct, and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency is judged by whether persons skilled in the art can, from the description (and permitted adjuncts), construct and use the invention without further inventive experiment. The description need not enable the general public or unskilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description of essential parts and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Each essential part of the invention must be clearly and exactly delineated, and the relation of each to the others definitely portrayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever features are indispensable to the invention's performance must be described in words as accurately as the case admits. Features not indispensable may be omitted. Details of shape, size, materials, proportion, arrangement are required only when essential to operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe one mode of reducing the idea to practical utility, and that mode must be the best one known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding for the inventor's or licensees' benefit a better form than the one disclosed is a fraud on the public and will render the patent void. The mode described must be the best within the inventor's knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one practicable embodiment required
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is not required to describe all possible embodiments, but must describe at least one practicable method of carrying the invention into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public, having one embodiment before it, is presumed able to construct others within ordinary mechanical skill. However, if other modes depend on additional inventive skill, they may be separate inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must disclose a definite mode of use (not just results)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must disclose a method of putting the invention to practical use and must prescribe fixed and definite rules of action by following which the given result will be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely asserting that a result can be obtained is insufficient. The mode explained must be the best known and must be described in such terms that practitioners can follow it to obtain the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description must be complete in itself; drawings/models are auxiliary
rubrics_metrics.description: The written Description must be complete in itself, although its language may be illustrated and applied by a model or drawings which accompany it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings or models may illustrate form or position of parts but cannot supply the place of a written description to the extent that a claim would cover matter indicated only by the drawings. A model cannot replace a written Description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new matter from prior art; disclose state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art to which the invention belongs must be sufficiently described to show its real place in the art and to disclose precise points in which it differs from previously known inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes the new matter to be covered by the patent from the old. When several inventions are joined, the same particularity is necessary for each; when invention is generic, at least one species must be delineated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit description to descriptive matter, avoid argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description ought to be confined to the three required subjects; matters beyond these are surplusage and objectionable, especially praise of the invention or disparagement of competing inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications should be descriptive, not argumentative. Assertions of superiority or eulogistic matter are immaterial and out of place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency judged by persons skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must be sufficient for persons skilled in the art; it is addressed to artisans with ordinary and fair information in the particular art, not to the unskilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and examiners assume readers will bring ordinary knowledge of the art. A specification that enables those skilled in the art satisfies the law even if unintelligible to the unskilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may assume contemporary common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is addressed to persons skilled in the art as the art existed at the date of the invention and may assume knowledge of that prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Description cannot be supplemented by knowledge of subsequent discoveries or another's later invention. If, on the assumption that certain matters are known to skilled persons, the specification is intelligible, it is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of specification as a whole (read with adjuncts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description is sufficient if, when read with drawings, the model, petition, oath, and other parts of the application, the invention can be ascertained by those to whom the specification is addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents are construed as a whole; imperfections in one part may be interpreted or corrected by others. Courts look at the whole description and accompanying papers to determine sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness: description must correspond to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of each subject-matter must be correct, complete, and intelligible; correctness means that the words used correspond exactly with the real nature of the thing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether statements are true in fact is a jury question (fact). The court decides legal sufficiency. A description that corresponds in substance with the invention is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to describe essential elements is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: A failure to describe an essential element renders the patent useless to the public and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential necessary means must be described, not mere accidental adjuncts. Omission of an element without which the new machine will work may or may not be fatal depending on whether the missing element is within the inventor's conception as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must describe property on which utility depends
rubrics_metrics.description: When the utility of an invention is dependent on some property of matter, the Description must describe that property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention's usefulness depends on a particular material property (e.g., a chemical property), that property must be disclosed; the patentee is bound by the qualities that actually exist in the produced article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory or scientific principle need not be explained
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to explain the scientific theory or principle on which the invention operates; abstract or theoretical principles need not be mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor need not understand the theory, nor is such knowledge necessary for the public to use the invention; description of means and mode is what matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of best mode invalidates patent
rubrics_metrics.description: To conceal the best mode of applying the principle of the invention for the benefit of the inventor or his licensees avoids the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor must disclose the best mode known; deliberate concealment of a superior embodiment can be treated as fraud on the public and render the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of result alone do not satisfy description
rubrics_metrics.description: A description that merely states a result without disclosing the means by which it is attained does not describe the invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing only the outcome (a result) is inadequate; the specification must describe the means and method to achieve that result so a skilled person can practice it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple inventions in one application require particularity for each
rubrics_metrics.description: When several inventions are joined in one application, the same particularity of description is necessary in regard to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each distinct invention claimed must be described with sufficient specificity to enable practice; failure to do so for any joined invention risks invalidity for that invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes may be tolerable if the skilled mechanic can correct them
rubrics_metrics.description: An imperfect description or a mistake in describing some part of the machinery may not be fatal if it can be easily discovered or corrected by the mechanic or by other parts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that a description that is obscure or imperfect can still be sufficient if, looking at the whole patent and accompanying papers, the invention can be specified with reasonable certainty. Caveats and background history belong to the history of the invention rather than its required description.
